title: Post-CTS Routing Congestion Resolved via Macro Shifting and Localized NDR

observation.description: Post-CTS routing congestion spiked to 18% overflow in vertical channels between macro columns, with 850 routing shorts and 350 spacing violations.

hypothesis: The clock tree insertion created localized clock-routing blockages because the clock nets were routed on higher metal layers without considering the dense standard cell routing needs in the same vertical channels, effectively choking the signal routing resources.

candidates_considered.action: Increase block utilization to 88% and shrink the floorplan.
candidates_considered.rejected_because: It would exacerbate the existing 14% congestion and likely push overflow >25%, causing unrouteable hotspots and massive DRC violations.

candidates_considered.action: Rip up and re-run CTS with higher clock tree latency targets (skew relaxation).
candidates_considered.rejected_because: It would degrade WNS by at least 100ps, pushing timing into critical failure, and require a full re-optimization cycle costing 3 days of schedule.

candidates_considered.action: Add routing blockages on M5/M6 in the congested channels to force CTS to route clocks on M7/M8.
candidates_considered.rejected_because: M7/M8 are reserved for power straps in this 16nm kit; using them for signal routing violates the power grid methodology and causes severe IR drop issues.

chosen_intervention: Applied localized Non-Default Rules (NDR) to clock nets only in the congested regions to use wider wires on lower layers (M3/M4) while reducing the number of clock vias, and slightly shifted 5 large macros by 10um to break up the vertical routing channel alignment.
expert_assessment: Shifting macros to break routing channel alignment is a classic, low-risk floorplan tweak that avoids the severe penalties of full CTS re-runs. The lesson is to align macro placement with the natural routing grain early, rather than trying to fix it post-CTS. This wouldn't transfer well to a block with highly irregular macro placements or strict pinout constraints.
weakest_point: The exact DRC count reduction from 1200 to 45 via a 10um macro shift might be overly optimistic for a 16nm node where DRCs are often highly localized and stubborn.

title: Timing Cliff Identified as SDC Multicycle Path Error Rather Than Logic Delay

observation.description: Post-synthesis timing report showed 4,500 failing paths. 95% of them shared the same 3 sink pins, failing by exactly 0.35ns to 0.38ns.

hypothesis: The failure signature (massive path count, identical slack, identical endpoints) indicates an SDC constraint error rather than a physical/logic delay problem, because physical logic variations would yield a distribution of slack values, not a single sharp cliff at -0.35ns.

candidates_considered.action: Upsize the drivers on the 3 shared sink pins to reduce cell delay.
candidates_considered.rejected_because: It would add ~40% capacitance load to the preceding stage, shifting the bottleneck and likely degrading the overall WNS by another 50ps without fixing the root constraint mismatch.

candidates_considered.action: Re-run synthesis with higher effort and boundary optimization.
candidates_considered.rejected_because: The identical slack across 4,000+ paths is a mathematical signature of a constraint boundary issue, not a logic optimization plateau; re-running would just waste 12 hours of compute and yield the same cliff.

candidates_considered.action: Add a 50ps timing margin to the clock latency in the SDC.
candidates_considered.rejected_because: It masks the symptom without fixing the underlying path grouping, and would artificially tighten timing on the rest of the block, causing false failures in subsequent P&R.

chosen_intervention: Investigated the SDC and found that the 3 sink pins belonged to a synchronizer chain crossing a clock domain boundary, but the set_max_delay was missing the -datapath_only flag, causing the tool to check both the launching and capturing clock paths simultaneously against an impossible budget. Added the flag and excluded the first launching flop.
expert_assessment: Recognizing the 'cliff' in the timing report is a crucial senior skill; it prevents wasted cycles on physical fixes for constraint bugs. The general lesson is that when hundreds of paths fail by the exact same margin to the same endpoints, always check the SDC grouping before touching the RTL. This wouldn't transfer if the paths were failing across many different endpoints with a normal distribution of slack.
weakest_point: The exact slack value (-0.35ns) being identical across 4,500 paths is slightly idealized; in reality, there is usually a tiny variation (e.g., -0.34ns to -0.36ns) due to min/max delay variations in the library cells, even with a constraint error.

title: Block Boundary Timing Budget Reallocation from Receiving Block Margin

observation.description: Block boundary timing between Block A (processor) and Block B (memory controller) showed a setup violation of -100ps on the data bus, with 45 failing paths.

hypothesis: The 500ps budget originally allocated for the off-chip/board routing between the two blocks was too aggressive, leaving only 200ps for the internal block routing of Block A, which is physically impossible given the 2mm distance across the block.

candidates_considered.action: Increase the internal block routing budget for Block A from 200ps to 300ps by reducing the off-chip budget to 400ps.
candidates_considered.rejected_because: The board-level signal integrity team confirmed that 400ps is the absolute minimum required to meet the eye-diagram specs for the PCB traces; reducing it would cause system-level bit errors.

candidates_considered.action: Insert a synchronous FIFO (async boundary) between Block A and Block B to break the timing path.
candidates_considered.rejected_because: It would add 2 cycles of latency to the memory access path, violating the strict performance requirement for the processor's L2 cache miss penalty, and would require 3 weeks of RTL redesign and verification.

candidates_considered.action: Relax the clock skew constraint between the two blocks from 50ps to 150ps in the SDC.
candidates_considered.rejected_because: The two blocks share the same PLL, and the physical distance of the clock tree makes a 150ps skew physically unachievable without adding massive, area-prohibitive clock buffers that would violate the power budget.

chosen_intervention: Derived a new budget by reallocating 50ps from the memory controller's internal setup time (which had 120ps of margin) to the block boundary. Changed the SDC set_io_delay for the boundary to reflect a 450ps off-chip budget and 250ps internal budget, and added a specific set_false_path for the reverse direction (B to A) which was a status bus not critical for setup.
expert_assessment: Reallocating budget from a block with excess margin to a starved boundary is the correct hierarchical approach when system-level constraints are locked. The lesson is to always check the receiving block's internal margin before asking for system-level changes or RTL restructuring. This wouldn't transfer if both blocks were already at zero margin, which would have forced the FIFO insertion despite the latency penalty.
weakest_point: The assumption that the memory controller had exactly 120ps of internal margin to spare might be overly convenient; in practice, extracting margin from a hardened or tightly constrained memory controller often reveals hidden pessimism or requires re-optimizing its internal datapath.
